patient.chief_complaint: New seizure-like episodes over the past 2 months — different from prior epileptic seizures
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. F is a 42-year-old truck driver with established right temporal lobe epilepsy, seizure-free on levetiracetam for 4 years, who presents with 2-month history of new episodes that he and his wife describe as different from his prior seizures. His prior epileptic seizures consisted of right temporal aura (déjà vu, rising epigastric sensation), followed by unresponsiveness with oral automatisms (lip smacking, swallowing) lasting 60-90 seconds, and post-ictal confusion for 5-10 minutes. The new episodes are distinctly different: they consist of bilateral whole-body shaking with arched back (opisthotonus-like posturing), closed eyes, 2-5 minute duration, no post-ictal confusion, and immediate full recovery. His wife is convinced these are different from his prior seizures. His driving license was suspended when he reported new episodes, creating significant financial and psychological stress as trucking is his sole income source. He is desperate to have the episodes attributed to epilepsy (which is treatable and would support his disability claim) rather than to a functional cause. Levetiracetam level was checked by his PCP and was therapeutic. He has been compliant with medications. Prior MRI from 3 years ago showed right mesial temporal sclerosis (MTS). His diabetes is well-controlled. He has not had any prior PNES episodes.

Clinical correlation recommended.

results.title: PNES in patients with epilepsy: management and outcomes

output.summary: An estimated 25–30% of patients with psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES) have co-existing epilepsy, making mixed presentations a recognized diagnostic challenge. Video-EEG with event capture is the reference standard for characterising each event type and distinguishing epileptic from non-epileptic events. Published case series report that escalation of antiepileptic drug therapy does not reduce PNES frequency. Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) has demonstrated efficacy for PNES in randomised trials. Clinical correlation recommended.

differential.key_features: Levetiracetam therapeutic; video-EEG shows NO ictal correlate during new episode type; semiology completely different from known right TLE seizures (bilateral shaking vs unilateral temporal aura + automatisms); no post-ictal confusion

No ictal EEG correlate; immediate full recovery; not status by duration criteria with these episode characteristics

critical_actions: Video-EEG is MANDATORY in known epilepsy with new episode type — cannot diagnose PNES in epilepsy patient without event capture
Do NOT increase levetiracetam — PNES does not respond to AEDs
Communicate clearly that PNES and epilepsy are both present and require separate treatments
contraindicated_actions: Increasing levetiracetam or adding second AED without video-EEG confirmation of breakthrough epilepsy — will not help PNES and adds medication burden
Dismissing all episodes as PNES because patient has psychosocial stress — right TLE is still active and the patient's established epilepsy requires continued management
key_reasoning_points: 25-30% of PNES patients have concurrent epilepsy — mixed epilepsy + PNES is the single most common diagnostic challenge in epilepsy monitoring units
In mixed epilepsy + PNES, video-EEG is essential: epileptic seizures (right TLE here) show ictal onset at right temporal electrodes; PNES show no ictal correlate
Semiology change — new episode type completely different from established seizure semiology — is the KEY clinical clue to new PNES in a known epilepsy patient
Both conditions require separate management: continue levetiracetam for TLE; CBT-FND and neuropsychiatry for PNES

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Known epilepsy does not exclude superimposed PNES; the new episode semiology is completely different from established TLE; video-EEG shows no ictal correlate for new episode type
